Name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
SDKs & notable repos: SDKs for Python, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Rust; Inspector debugging tool
Downloadable / offline docs: Spec is a single readable document, versioned by date
Notes: The emerging standard for connecting models to tools and data. Read the spec directly — it is short, and it explains the trust boundaries most integrations get wrong.

Name: MCP reference servers
SDKs & notable repos: Reference implementations for filesystem, git, databases, fetch and more
Notes: Read two or three before writing your own. The patterns are not obvious from the spec alone.

Name: A2A (Agent2Agent)
SDKs & notable repos: Agent-to-agent communication: agent cards, task delegation, streaming
Notes: Complements MCP rather than competing with it — MCP connects agents to tools, A2A connects agents to each other. Linux Foundation governed.

Name: OpenAI function calling
SDKs & notable repos: The tool-call interface most frameworks ultimately target
Notes: Learn the raw protocol before adopting a framework. Most agent bugs are tool-schema bugs.

Name: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions
SDKs & notable repos: Standard span and attribute names for model calls, tool calls and agent steps
Notes: Instrument to this rather than a vendor SDK. It is the one observability choice that is hard to reverse.

Name: OpenAI Agents SDK
SDKs & notable repos: Agents, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, built-in tracing
Notes: Deliberately small. A good first framework precisely because it does not hide much.

Name: Claude Agent SDK
SDKs & notable repos: The harness behind Claude Code, exposed as a library; subagents, hooks, MCP
Notes: Unusually valuable because the production system built on it is one you can observe directly.

Name: LangGraph
SDKs & notable repos: Agents as explicit state graphs; checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, time travel
Notes: The graph model is the right abstraction once control flow matters. Durable checkpointing is the feature that makes agents operable.

Name: Pydantic AI
SDKs & notable repos: Type-safe agents with validated structured output and dependency injection
Notes: Feels like normal Python rather than a DSL. Strong choice if your codebase already uses Pydantic.

Name: smolagents
SDKs & notable repos: Minimal agent library centred on code-writing agents
Notes: About a thousand lines. Read the whole thing — it is the fastest way to understand what an agent loop actually is.

Name: CrewAI
SDKs & notable repos: Role-based multi-agent teams with tasks and processes

Name: AutoGen
SDKs & notable repos: Microsoft's multi-agent conversation framework; event-driven core
Notes: The most research-driven of the multi-agent frameworks; papers accompany the design.

Name: Semantic Kernel
SDKs & notable repos: Enterprise-oriented orchestration for .NET, Python and Java

Name: Google Agent Development Kit
SDKs & notable repos: Google's agent framework; multi-agent, evaluation, deployment to Vertex

Name: LlamaIndex Workflows
SDKs & notable repos: Event-driven agent workflows with strong retrieval integration

Name: Mastra
SDKs & notable repos: TypeScript agent framework: workflows, RAG, evals
Notes: The most complete option if your stack is TypeScript rather than Python.

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: Claude Code
SDKs & notable repos: Terminal coding agent; hooks, subagents, MCP, skills
Notes: Study the hooks and permissions model — it is a worked answer to 'how do you let an agent act without letting it act freely'.

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: OpenHands
SDKs & notable repos: Open-source software-development agent with a sandboxed runtime
Notes: Fully open and genuinely capable. The runtime isolation design is the part to read.

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: SWE-agent
SDKs & notable repos: The Princeton research agent that established the agent-computer interface idea
Notes: The ACI paper is the key insight: agent performance depends more on tool design than on prompting.

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: Aider
SDKs & notable repos: Terminal pair programmer with repository mapping and git integration
Notes: The repo-map approach to context selection is clever and well documented.

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: Cline
SDKs & notable repos: Autonomous coding agent in VS Code with plan/act separation

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: Continue

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: browser-use
SDKs & notable repos: Agents that drive a real browser via the accessibility tree

Category: 3. Coding agents — read these, they are the most mature
Name: Playwright MCP
SDKs & notable repos: Browser automation exposed as an MCP server
Notes: Uses the accessibility tree rather than screenshots — far more reliable than vision-based clicking.

Name: E2B
SDKs & notable repos: Firecracker-backed sandboxes for running agent-generated code
Notes: If your agent executes code it wrote, it needs one of these. Not optional.

Name: Modal
SDKs & notable repos: Serverless containers with fast cold starts; common agent execution backend

Name: Temporal
SDKs & notable repos: Durable execution — workflows that survive crashes and restarts
Notes: The right substrate for long-running agents. Agent loops are workflows, and most frameworks reinvent this badly.

Name: LangGraph persistence
Notes: The closest thing to durable execution inside an agent framework itself.

Name: Langfuse
SDKs & notable repos: Open-source tracing for multi-step agent runs; self-hostable
Notes: Agent debugging is trace debugging. Without this you are reading logs and guessing.

Name: OpenLLMetry
SDKs & notable repos: OpenTelemetry instrumentation for LLM and agent frameworks

Name: Inspect AI
SDKs & notable repos: Evaluation framework with first-class agent and tool support
Notes: From the UK AI Safety Institute. The most rigorous open framework for evaluating agents.

Name: SWE-bench
SDKs & notable repos: Real GitHub issues from real repositories; the dominant coding-agent benchmark
Downloadable / offline docs: Harness and datasets in the repo
Notes: Verified, Lite and Full are different benchmarks. Scores get quoted without saying which — always check.

Name: Terminal-Bench
SDKs & notable repos: Agents operating a real terminal on real tasks
Notes: Less saturated than SWE-bench and harder to game.

Name: Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard
Notes: The most useful single signal for whether a model can call tools reliably.

Name: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
SDKs & notable repos: 'Excessive agency' and 'insecure output handling' are the agent-specific entries
Notes: Agents turn prompt injection from an information-disclosure bug into a remote-code-execution bug. Read this first.

Name: Simon Willison — the lethal trifecta
SDKs & notable repos: Private data + untrusted content + external communication = unsafe, regardless of prompting
Notes: The single most useful design rule in agent engineering. Remove one leg of the trifecta.

Name: MITRE ATLAS
Notes: Use it to structure an agent threat model.

Name: arXiv
SDKs & notable repos: Preprints across all of CS; most systems, ML and PL work appears here before publication
Downloadable / offline docs: Every paper is a free PDF. Bulk access documented at https://info.arxiv.org/help/bulk_data/index.html; a full-text API at export.arxiv.org
Notes: Not peer-reviewed. Treat an arXiv-only paper as a claim, not a result — but it is where you will read almost everything first.

Name: ar5iv
SDKs & notable repos: Renders any arXiv paper as responsive HTML instead of PDF
Notes: Makes papers readable on a phone and searchable in-page. Underused.

Name: alphaXiv
SDKs & notable repos: arXiv papers with a public comment and discussion layer
Notes: Useful when a paper is contested — the discussion often contains the critique you were looking for.

Name: Semantic Scholar
SDKs & notable repos: 200M+ papers with citation graph, influential-citation scoring and TLDR summaries
Downloadable / offline docs: Free Graph API (https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api), bulk datasets available on request
Notes: The best free citation graph. 'Highly influential citations' is a genuinely useful filter for finding what actually mattered.

Name: OpenAlex
SDKs & notable repos: Fully open catalogue of works, authors, venues and institutions; successor to Microsoft Academic Graph
Downloadable / offline docs: Entirely free API with no key required; complete database snapshots downloadable
Notes: The only large-scale bibliographic database that is open all the way down, including bulk snapshots.

Name: DBLP
SDKs & notable repos: Authoritative CS bibliography — complete author and venue listings
Notes: The fastest way to find everything a given researcher has published, and to see a conference's full programme by year.

Name: OpenReview
SDKs & notable repos: ICLR, NeurIPS, COLM and dozens of other venues — papers plus the full review threads
Notes: Reading the reviews and author rebuttals teaches you how the field evaluates work. Nothing else exposes this.

Name: CORE
SDKs & notable repos: Aggregates 300M+ open-access papers from repositories worldwide
Notes: Good for finding the green open-access copy when a publisher's version is paywalled.

Name: Unpaywall
SDKs & notable repos: Finds legal free copies of paywalled papers via DOI
Notes: Legal, author-deposited copies only. Install the extension and most paywalls simply stop appearing.

Name: Papers We Love
SDKs & notable repos: A curated, categorised repository of classic CS papers with local meetup talks
Downloadable / offline docs: Repo cloneable; many PDFs mirrored in-repo
Notes: The best starting point if you do not yet know which papers matter in a subfield.

Name: The Morning Paper (archive)
Notes: No longer updated, but the back catalogue of ~1000 summarised papers is one of the great free CS resources.

Name: USENIX Proceedings
SDKs & notable repos: OSDI, SOSP (co-published), NSDI, ATC, FAST, Security — the core systems venues
Downloadable / offline docs: Every paper free, immediately, with no membership. Often with recorded talks
Notes: USENIX made everything open access years before the rest of the field. If a systems paper exists, check here first.

Name: ACM Digital Library
SDKs & notable repos: SIGMOD, ASPLOS, PLDI, POPL, SoCC and the ACM journals
Downloadable / offline docs: Partly open: ACM Open and author-paid OA papers are free; others are paywalled
Notes: 403s to automated clients; loads in a browser. For paywalled items, check arXiv, the author's homepage or Unpaywall first — the free copy usually exists.

Name: IEEE Xplore
SDKs & notable repos: ISCA, MICRO, HPCA and the IEEE journals
Notes: Almost always worth searching the author's page or arXiv instead. Architecture authors in particular post preprints widely.

Name: DROPS / LIPIcs (Dagstuhl)
SDKs & notable repos: ECOOP, ITP, CONCUR, SAT and many theory venues
Downloadable / offline docs: 100% open access, free PDFs, Creative Commons licensed
Notes: A fully open publisher. Every paper, always free, no exceptions.

Name: arXiv cs.AI / cs.MA
SDKs & notable repos: Agent architectures and multi-agent systems. See also https://arxiv.org/list/cs.MA/recent
Notes: Agent papers are overwhelmingly preprints; very little is peer reviewed yet.

Name: arXiv cs.SE (Software Engineering)
SDKs & notable repos: Coding agents, program repair, SWE-bench-style evaluation
Notes: Where the coding-agent literature actually lives — easy to miss if you only watch cs.AI.

Name: ACL Anthology
SDKs & notable repos: Tool use, ReAct-lineage and dialogue-agent work, peer reviewed

Name: COLM
SDKs & notable repos: Language-modelling venue carrying a growing share of agent work

Name: OpenReview
SDKs & notable repos: Reviews and rebuttals for agent papers
Notes: Agent benchmarks attract methodological criticism; the reviews are where you find it.

Name: SWE-bench
SDKs & notable repos: The dominant coding-agent benchmark, with a public leaderboard
Notes: Read the harness before believing a score. Verified, Lite and Full are different tasks and get conflated constantly.

Name: Terminal-Bench
SDKs & notable repos: Benchmark for agents operating a real terminal
Notes: Harder and less saturated than SWE-bench.

Name: Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard
SDKs & notable repos: Standardised evaluation of tool- and function-calling ability
Notes: The most useful single number for 'can this model call tools reliably'.

Name: Hugging Face Papers
SDKs & notable repos: Daily curation, usually with the agent repos linked

Name: Anthropic Engineering
Notes: Currently the best-written practical material on agent design from any lab.

Name: Google DeepMind publications
SDKs & notable repos: Planning, tool use and multi-agent research

Name: USENIX Proceedings
SDKs & notable repos: Where the systems and security consequences of agents are starting to appear
Notes: As agents get deployment surface, the serious failure analysis will land here rather than at ML venues.

Name: Building Effective Agents (Anthropic)
SDKs & notable repos: Read this before you pick a framework
Notes: The most useful thing written on this topic. Its central argument — that most problems need a workflow, not an agent, and that you should start with the simplest thing that works — will save you months.

Name: ReAct paper
SDKs & notable repos: Read this before you pick a framework
Notes: The reasoning-and-acting loop every framework is a variation on. Short.

Name: smolagents
SDKs & notable repos: Read this before you pick a framework
Notes: About a thousand lines. Read it end to end and the magic disappears — an agent is a loop, a tool schema, and a stopping condition.

Notes: The emerging standard for tool and data access. Learn it before any framework's bespoke tool abstraction.

Notes: Read two or three before writing your own.

Name: Pydantic AI
Notes: Type-safe and idiomatic Python. Good if you want validation from day one.

Notes: Multi-agent composition plus a deployment story.

Name: A2A protocol

Name: Aider repository map

Notes: The ACI argument: design the tools for the model, not for the human.

Name: tree-sitter
Notes: The parsing layer under most code-aware context selection. See the compilers index.

Notes: Firecracker microVMs per sandbox. Read the architecture, not just the SDK.

Notes: The deeper guides beyond the Top 10 list, including agentic-specific material.

Notes: Probe your deployed agent, including tool-abuse paths.

Notes: Automated red-teaming with orchestrators and converters.

Notes: Action rails — constraining what an agent may do, not just what it may say.
